Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:12: On the night after the fast, one should be careful not to fill his belly with meat and wine, lest his heart grow haughty and he lose his gain through this loss; and a penitent must distance himself from these, especially from wine, as they said in the Zohar (parashat Miketz 202a): as for what is said, that a person should remember the day of death — surely this is so, because it breaks a person's heart, for the evil inclination rests only in a place where the joy of wine and haughtiness of spirit are found; and when it finds a broken spirit, it then separates from him and does not rest with him. — end of quotation. And since it says "haughtiness of spirit," one must distance himself from pleasures so that his spirit not come to grow haughty over him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:13: Many Torah scholars of our generation rely on not fasting, based on the statement (Ta'anit 11a) that Shmuel said, whoever sits in a fast is called a sinner, holding like the view of the Tanna who taught: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar the son of Rabbi says, why does it say (Numbers 6:11), "and he shall atone for him for having sinned regarding the soul" — but against which soul did this [Nazirite] sin? Rather, he afflicted himself by abstaining from wine — and by an a fortiori argument: if this one, who only afflicted himself by abstaining from wine, is called a sinner, how much more so one who afflicts himself from everything! Rabbi Elazar says, he is called holy, as it is said (ibid. 6:5), "he shall be holy, he shall let the locks of hair on his head grow long" — and if this one, who only afflicted himself in one matter, is called holy, how much more so one who afflicts himself from everything! And according to Shmuel, is he then called holy — that one who purifies his soul [via abstinence]? And according to Rabbi Elazar, is he then called a sinner — that one who defiles his soul? But did Rabbi Elazar say this? Did not Rabbi Elazar say, a person should always regard himself as though a holy one dwelt within his innards, as it is said (Hosea 11:9), "the Holy One is within you, and I will not come into the city"? This is not difficult — the one case is where he can afflict himself [without harm]; the other is where he cannot afflict himself. Reish Lakish said, he is called a chasid, as it is said (Proverbs 11:17), "the pious man rewards his own soul." Rav Sheshet said, this student of the academy who sits in a fast — let the dog eat his portion [i.e., it is worthless]! Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba said, there is no communal fast in Babylonia except the Ninth of Av alone. Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba said in the name of Reish Lakish, a Torah scholar is not permitted to sit in a fast, because he thereby diminishes the work of Heaven. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:14: From this last statement of Reish Lakish, support is drawn for not fasting, and as Rashi, peace be upon him, explained — "he diminishes the work of Heaven" — he becomes weak and cannot study. — end of quotation. Since he is weak and cannot study, he is termed "unable to afflict himself," and is called a sinner; and Reish Lakish's statement, that he is called a chasid, as it is said, "the pious man rewards his own soul," must be reconciled, according to their view, as referring to one who can afflict himself, or to one who is not a Torah scholar, so that Reish Lakish not contradict himself, since he also said, a Torah scholar is not permitted to sit in a fast.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:15: None of this supports one who has sinned, that he should not fast and that Torah alone should suffice to atone for his sin — for whoever has sinned, even if he is a Torah scholar, his Torah is not accepted until he purifies himself, as explained at the end of chapter 2, and the proof of this is Reish Lakish himself, who is explained in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (ch. 42), which we quoted above (ch. 3), that after he repented, all his days he was engaged in fasting, charity, and prayer. Rather, surely Reish Lakish's words are said only regarding a Torah scholar who has not sinned — that if he wishes to fast in order to sanctify himself, he is not permitted, because he diminishes the work of Heaven — but if he has sinned and sits in a fast, he is called a chasid, as it is said, "the pious man rewards his own soul" — and the explanation of "rewards his own soul" is that he repays his soul, paying it back according to its measure, in the manner the verse says (Psalms 62:13), "and to You, O Lord, is kindness, for You repay each man according to his deed" — thus with the attribute of Chesed, a man is repaid according to his deed. And so it is explained that through accepting sufferings he draws himself near to Chesed, as it is said (Proverbs 13:24), "but he who loves him disciplines him early" — and love is the love of Chesed, and simple purity is from the side of Chesed, as we explained above (ch. 3).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:16: Further, we say in the Yerushalmi, Nedarim, chapter Konam (ch. 8, halachah 1): Rabbi Yonatan used to fast every eve of Rosh Hashanah; Rabbi Avin used to fast every eve of Shabbat; Rabbi Ze'ira fasted three hundred fasts — some say nine hundred fasts — and did not concern himself with Megillat Ta'anit [the scroll listing days when fasting is forbidden]. — end of quotation. And so it is found in the Yerushalmi, Ta'aniyot, chapter 2 (halachah 12).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:17: So too the Tur wrote (Laws of Shabbat, siman 249): one does not fix a meal on the eve of Shabbat because of the honor of Shabbat, and he writes afterward, and it appears that the custom of men of deeds was to fast the whole day, as it is stated in Eruvin (40b): those students of the master who were sitting in a fast on the eve of Shabbat, what of completing it? — thus it is the way of Torah scholars to fast on the eve of Shabbat. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:18: Also, one should not bring proof from what we say in Ta'aniyot (22b): Rabbi Yosi says, an individual is not permitted to afflict himself with fasting lest he become a burden on the community — for this is resolved by what the Ran, of blessed memory, wrote there. He already explained above that because they fast on these [communal calamities] consecutively, he [Rabbi Yosi] says that an individual is not permitted to fast on these consecutively. The explanation of his words, that he said "because they fast on these consecutively" — the intent is what is said there: our rabbis taught, a city surrounded by troops, or by a river, or a ship tossed at sea, or an individual pursued by gentiles or by an evil spirit or by bandits — they sound the alarm immediately, even on Shabbat, and regarding all of these an individual is not permitted to afflict himself with fasting, lest he become a burden on the community, and the community not have mercy on him. Here, Rabbi Yosi is responding to the words of the first Tanna, who spoke of afflicting oneself with fasts for another's sake — such as praying for a city surrounded by troops or for an individual pursued — and as the Ran explained, that regarding these it is permitted to fast consecutively, and it is regarding these that Rabbi Yosi disagrees and says he should not fast consecutively, because he would neglect his work, etc. — but regarding one who fasts consecutively for repentance for his own sins, Rabbi Yosi did not speak of this.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:19: On the contrary, a blessing of good shall come upon him — for in Tractate Yoma (86b), Mar Zutra bar Toviah said in the name of Rav, great is repentance, for even if an individual performs it, it is forgiven for him and for the whole world, as it is said (Hosea 14:5), "I will heal their backsliding." And not only that, but it brings healing to the world, as we say there (86a): Rabbi said, great is repentance, for it brings healing to the world, as it is said (Jeremiah 3:22), "return, backsliding children, I will heal your backslidings." And if repentance has the power to bring healing to the world, how much more so to himself, that it bring healing so that he be healthy and not become ill. And should you say that repentance is possible without fasting — the prophet has already explicitly stated the conditions of repentance (Joel 2:12), "with all your heart, with fasting and with weeping and with mourning."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:20: Further, they said in Midrash Mishlei on the verse (Proverbs 6:4), "give no sleep to your eyes" — in these words: give no sleep to your eyes without engaging in Torah, which atones for sin. Another interpretation: give no sleep to your eyes without performing repentance, for repentance and good deeds are like a shield against calamity. Another interpretation: give no sleep to your eyes without sitting in a fast, for fasting is close to repentance, as it is said (Joel 2:12-13), "and rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God" — if you do this, for He is gracious and merciful. And why all this? In order to be saved from the judgment of Gehinnom. Regarding this it is explained in the tradition (Proverbs 6:5), "free yourself like a gazelle from the hand, and like a bird from the hand of the fowler" — so that you not be caught up in the descent into Gehinnom. Another interpretation, "and like a bird from the hand of the fowler" — that you not become chaff [kash, wordplay] for the fire of Gehinnom — because the power of repentance reaches to the Throne of Glory. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:21: Here it is said that fasting is close to repentance, and the reason is as explained above at the beginning of this chapter. Therefore we find that for every distress that might come upon the community, a fast is decreed, as we learn in the first chapter of Ta'aniyot (1:4): if the seventeenth of Cheshvan arrived and rain had not fallen, individuals would begin to fast — and why should they fast? Would it not be better for them to engage in Torah, which atones for sin, and to examine their deeds, without fasting? Rather, fasting is necessary in order to bring about humility, and once he is sanctified from eating and drinking, which are the powers of the body, he clings to Him, blessed be He, and to His ministers, who are separated and holy from eating and drinking, and then He answers us because we are bound to Him — but through eating and drinking we are separated from Him, except when eating is a commandment, as on Shabbat and festivals and Rosh Chodesh and the like.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:22: Perhaps for this reason Mar, the son of Ravina, sat in a fast all year, as we say in Pesachim (68b): Mar, the son of Ravina, sat in a fast the entire year, except for Shavuot, Purim, and the eve of Yom Kippur.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:23: Whoever cannot fast the entire year consecutively should at least strive to fulfill the words of Rabbi Yaakov, the author of the Tur (Orach Chaim, siman 580), in these words: it is written in Halachot Gedolot: these are the days on which one fasts by Torah law, and one who fasts on them shall not eat or drink until evening — on the first of Nisan, the sons of Aaron died, etc. — and he writes at the end of his words: these days of fasting Israel received from the Torah, and further they decreed that they should fast for three reasons — Monday and Thursday and Monday — for the destruction of the Temple, for the burning of the Torah, and for the desecration of the Lord's Name; and in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to turn them into joy and gladness. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:24: So too they said in Tractate Sofrim, that the students fast on Monday and Thursday in Nisan, and the reason is because of our sages' decree regarding the three matters mentioned. In these words, chapter final, halachah 3: therefore they do not say Tachanun throughout the days of Nisan, and one does not fast until Nisan has passed — except for the firstborn, who fast on the eve of Passover, and the pious, for the sake of the matzah, so that they enter into it with appetite; and the students fast on it, Monday and Thursday, because of the desecration of the Name and because of the honor of the Sanctuary that was burned — this applies when done privately, but to mention it publicly is forbidden until Nisan has passed. — end of quotation. Here it is permitted for students to fast Monday and Thursday in Nisan because of the desecration of the Name, and the reason is that since this was their custom throughout the year, it teaches us that they do not stop in Nisan.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:25: The Tosafot wrote (Bava Kama 82a, s.v. "kedei") regarding what we say, that Ezra instituted that they read from the Torah on Monday and Thursday so that they not go three days without Torah — and should you ask, why specifically Monday and Thursday? One may say that it is because we say in the Midrash that Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, ascended on a Thursday to receive the second tablets, and descended on a Monday, and the Omnipresent was reconciled with him — and since it was a time of favor during that ascent and descent, they fixed [these readings] on Monday and Thursday, and therefore it also became the custom to fast on Monday and Thursday. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:26: Besides Monday and Thursday, there are days Israel has been accustomed to fast: on the eve of Rosh Chodesh they are accustomed to fast, and they say it is a "minor Yom Kippur" — and the reason for this fast is that it is known that Israel counts by the moon, as explained in the Zohar (parashat Vayechi, beginning of pp. 236b-237a), because this moon alludes to the supernal moon [Malchut], and since there is diminishment and lack below, so above; and the righteous, who suffer through the sufferings of the Shechinah, accepting the judgment that comes upon her, when she renews herself, they too renew themselves with her.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:27: So too they said in the Zohar (parashat Vayeshev 181a) regarding the righteous who have sufferings because they were born in the diminishment of the moon — that in the future they have a great rank, and the Shechinah never departs from them, in these words there: and when the moon is blemished, on that side of the evil serpent, then all those souls that come out, although they are all pure and all holy, since they come out amid blemish, in all those places those souls reach, all of them are broken and blemished with several distresses and several pains — and these are the souls in whom the Holy One, blessed be He, delights after they were broken, and although the souls are in sadness and not in joy, the secret of the matter rests in the manner of what is above — the body is blemished, and the soul within it, in the manner of what is above — surely in this manner. And therefore these are the ones who wish to be renewed with the renewal of the moon, and of these it is written (Isaiah 66:23), "and it shall come to pass that from new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before Me, says the Lord" — "all flesh" indeed, for these shall be renewed in everything, and wish to be renewed with the renewal of the moon; and these are partnered together with the moon, blemished with her blemish, and therefore she dwells among them always, not abandoning them, in the manner of (Isaiah 57:15), "and with the contrite and lowly of spirit," and it is written (Psalms 34:19), "the Lord is near to the brokenhearted" — to those who bore that blemish along with the moon — they are always near to her, and therefore, "to revive the heart of the contrite ones," in that life that comes to her to be renewed, this shall be their portion: those who bore [suffering] with her shall be renewed with her — and these are called "sufferings of love" — for they are of love, and it does not depend on that person — they are of love, because the light of the small love [Malchut] that was pushed away from the great love [Tiferet] was blemished — and therefore these are companions partnered with her; happy is their portion in this world and in the World to Come, that they have merited this — to be companions with her — of them it is written (Psalms 122:8), "for the sake of my brothers and friends," etc. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:28: From here we learn that whoever suffers along with the Shechinah's distress has great reward, as explained in the passage, that "the Lord is near to the brokenhearted," to those who bore that blemish along with the moon, etc. — it appears that whoever afflicts himself with sufferings and breaks his heart is renewed with her. Therefore, on the eve of Rosh Chodesh, when she is entirely blemished, it is fitting to afflict oneself and fast. And with every fast one performs, it is good that he intend this as well — beyond the fact that through his sin he caused her affliction, as we elaborated at length in the Gate of Fear, that "a foolish son is his mother's grief" — therefore it is fitting that he suffer affliction in exchange for the affliction he caused her, all the more so now, in this our exile, when because of our transgressions our mother was sent away — it is fitting for every person to suffer along with her distress and accept sufferings for having prolonged the exile through our sins; and on the matter of humility we have elaborated further; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:29: Further, there are days Israel has been accustomed to fast, such as from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Yom Kippur, which are days on which Selichot and supplications are said, and they relied on this: (Song of Songs 6:3), "Ani LeDodi VeDodi Li" — whose initial letters spell "Elul" and whose final letters are four yods, corresponding to the forty days; and likewise (Deuteronomy 30:6), "and the Lord your God will circumcise Et Levavcha VeEt Levav" — initial letters spelling "Elul" — that this month is prepared for the circumcision of the heart, that is, repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:30: It stands to reason, since it is the last month of the year, to perform in it repentance for what one blemished throughout the whole year, so that he not enter Rosh Hashanah, the day of judgment, defiled by his evil deeds, but rather rectify in this month what has passed. And likewise, regarding the Ten Days of Repentance, their very name proves that they were instituted for the rectification of the year, and they are days of judgment on which we say "the King of Judgment," and the Holy One, blessed be He, makes Himself available then to receive penitents, as our sages, of blessed memory, expounded, "seek the Lord while He may be found" (Isaiah 55:6) — are there then days when He is not found? Rather, this refers to the individual, etc. — for during these days, even for the individual, He is found — and it is fitting to fast and examine one's deeds and fulfill the essential conditions of repentance, with all one's heart, with fasting and with weeping and with mourning; and at night one should not eat meat or drink wine.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:31: Rabbeinu Yonah wrote in Sha'arei Teshuvah (second gate, letter 14), in these words: during the Ten Days of Repentance, one who fears the word of the Lord — his heart shall tremble within him, knowing that all his deeds are recorded in a book, and at that time God shall bring into judgment every deed, regarding every hidden thing, whether good or evil — for man is judged on Rosh Hashanah, and his verdict is sealed on Yom Kippur; and when a man knows that his case will be brought before a king of flesh and blood, will he not tremble greatly and take counsel with his own soul, and by every diligent means hasten to find escape for himself, and it will not occur to his spirit to turn to the right or to the left and occupy himself with other matters? Therefore, how foolish are those who go out to their work and their labor until evening during these awesome days, the days of judgment and verdict, not knowing what their judgment will be! It is fitting for every God-fearing person to reduce his affairs and have his thoughts fixed, and to set times, day and night, to seclude himself in his chambers, to search his ways and investigate them, and to rise before dawn to engage in the ways of repentance and proper deeds, and to pour out his meditation and offer prayer and joyful song and cast down supplication — for the time is a time of favor, and prayer is heard within it. And our sages, of blessed memory, said, "seek the Lord while He may be found" — these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:32: It is a positive commandment from the Torah for a person to arouse his own spirit and return in repentance on Yom Kippur, as it is said (Leviticus 16:30), "from all your sins before the Lord you shall be purified" — and our sages, of blessed memory, said that Yom Kippur atones together with repentance; therefore Scripture warns us to purify ourselves before the Lord through our repentance, and He shall atone for us on this day, to purify us. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:33: When the discerning person contemplates the stories mentioned in the Gemara about sages who fasted several fasts, and sees that the matter was without so great a necessity, his soul will be enflamed to fast for all his sins, and each person knows what sins have preceded him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:34: The Rosh wrote in the Halachot Ketanot appended to Rabbi Yitzchak Alfasi's work (p. 8a), regarding what we say (Menachot 35b), Rav Ashi was sitting before Mar Zutra when his tefillin strap turned around — in these words, from the responsum of a Gaon: regarding Rav Huna's strap that turned around, and he sat forty days in a fast — whether it was the hand-tefillin strap or the head-tefillin strap — thus we have learned from our masters, that it was the head-tefillin strap; Rav Huna, who sat in a fast, did not do so because it was strictly obligatory, etc. And this incident of Rav Huna is brought in the Gemara of Tractate Mo'ed Katan (25a). And he wrote another responsum: whoever turns the head-tefillin or hand-tefillin strap around is obligated to sit in a fast, for he is negligent and needs a fast — but to obligate him to forty fasts like Rav Huna, no — this Rav Huna did out of extreme piety. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:35: So too we find that Rabbi Ze'ira fasted a hundred fasts so that the fire of Gehinnom not have power over him, as is stated in the Gemara (Bava Metzia 85a), besides two hundred others he fasted, as explained there. Also in the Yerushalmi (Shabbat, ch. 5, halachah 4), regarding what we say, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah's cow used to go out with a strap — our sages, of blessed memory, said: Rabbi Chanina said, once she went out and his teeth had blackened from the fasts. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:36: Also, if a Torah scholar fasts so that Torah be maintained within him and not cease from his descendants, it is good for him, as is stated there in "HaSocher et HaPo'alim" (85a), regarding what we say: Rabbi Peranch said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, whoever is a Torah scholar, and his son is a Torah scholar, and his grandson is a Torah scholar, Torah will never again cease from his descendants, as it is said (Isaiah 59:21), "and as for Me, this is My covenant with them," etc. Rav Yosef sat forty fasts, and they read to him, "they shall not depart from your mouth"; he sat another forty fasts, and they read to him, "and from the mouth of your seed"; he sat another hundred fasts, and they read to him, "they shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, nor from the mouth of your seed's seed." He said, from now on I need no more — Torah returns to its own lodging place. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:37: So too we find that Solomon fasted forty fasts for wisdom, as is stated at the beginning of Midrash Mishlei, on the reason the Book of Proverbs begins with the letter mem.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:38: Regarding the secret of fasting, it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Shemot 20a-b) — it says there, on the verse (Song of Songs 2:16), "my beloved is mine and I am his, who feeds among the roses" — that the Holy One, blessed be He, conducts His world with kindness and judgment, and the roses hint at this, having both redness and whiteness, in these words: what is this rose — red and white? So the fragrance of the sacrifice is from red and white. Come and see, from the fragrance of the incense, whose spices are some white and some red, such as the frankincense, which is white, and the free-flowing myrrh, which is red — and the fragrance ascends from red and white; therefore He conducts His world like roses, red and white, as it is written (Ezekiel 44:15), "to offer to Me fat and blood." Corresponding to this, a person offers his fat and blood and is atoned for — this is red and this is white. Just as the rose, which is red and white, cannot be shrunk to become entirely white except through fire, so the sacrifice cannot be shrunk to become entirely white except through fire. Now, one who sits in his fast and offers his fat and blood is not shrunk to become entirely white except through fire, for Rabbi Yehudah said, through a person's fast his limbs are weakened and the fire [of his body's heat] overpowers him, and at that moment he must offer his fat and blood in that very fire, and this is called the altar of atonement. This is what Rabbi Elazar said, when he would sit, he would pray and say: it is revealed and known before You, O Lord my God and God of my fathers, that I have offered before You my fat and my blood, and heated them with the heat of my body's weakness — may it be Your will that the fragrance rising from my mouth at this time be like the fragrance rising from the sacrifice on the fire of the altar, and be pleased with me. It follows that a person who offers, in his fast, the fat, the blood, and the fire, and the fragrance that rises — this is an altar of atonement. Therefore they instituted prayer in place of the sacrifice, provided that one intends what we have said. Rabbi Yitzchak said, from here on it is written (Numbers 31:23), "everything that can withstand fire, you shall pass through fire, and it shall be pure." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:39: Further, one should intend what is said in the Zohar, parashat Terumah (153a): there are three rulers above by which the Holy One, blessed be He, is known, and they are His precious secret — these are the brain, the heart, and the liver — and they are in reverse order from this world. Above, the brain takes first and gives afterward to the heart, and the heart takes and gives to the liver, and afterward the liver gives a portion to all those sources below, each and every one as is fitting for it. Below, the liver takes first, and afterward it brings everything near to the heart, and the heart takes it; once the heart takes it and is strengthened by that strength and desire it took, it is aroused toward the brain, and afterward the liver returns and divides the nourishment to all the limbs of the body. On the day of a fast, a person brings his food and drink near to the supernal liver, bringing near his fat, his blood, and his will; that liver takes everything with desire; once everything is with it, it takes and offers everything to the heart, which is great and rules over it; once the heart takes it and is strengthened with desire, it brings everything near to the brain, which is the supernal ruler over the whole body; afterward the liver returns and divides portions to all those sources and limbs below. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:40: Whoever contemplates the words of this passage will see with the eye of knowledge that fasting is literally a sacrifice, the secret of "a fire-offering, a pleasing aroma to the Lord" (Leviticus 1:9), as explained in the Zohar Chadash on Song of Songs. Therefore one must be careful on the day of the fast against every sin and iniquity, so that his sacrifice not be rejected, and he should judge from the things that disqualify a sacrifice, one of which is improper thought — for these will also disqualify a fast if he has improper thoughts of transgression. Likewise, other things that disqualify a sacrifice will disqualify a fast; therefore the abandonment of sin is needed, so that he not be like one who immerses while still holding an impure creeping thing in his hand.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:41: In Tractate Berachot (32b), regarding fasting, our sages, of blessed memory, said, and Rabbi Elazar said, fasting is greater than charity — why? Because this one is with his body and that one is with his money. — end of quotation. And saying "fasting is greater," etc., he thereby teaches us the merit of charity — for one does not say "this is greater than that" unless they belong to the same category and value. The reason is that charity atones for sin, as it says (Daniel 4), "and redeem your sin with charity," and likewise fasting is in place of the sacrifice and atones for sin, as they said there, chapter "Hayah Korei" (Berachot 17a): Rav Sheshet, when he sat in a fast, after praying he would say this: Master of the worlds, it is revealed before You that when the Temple stood, a person would sin and offer a sacrifice, and only his fat and blood would be offered from it, and he would be atoned for; and now I have sat in a fast, and my fat and blood have been diminished — may it be Your will that my fat and blood which were diminished be considered as though I had offered them before You upon the altar, and be pleased with me. — end of quotation. And fasting has an advantage over charity in that it is with his body, for he offers a person's face above — and just as at the time the Temple stood, in the performance of the sacrifice, the essence of the sacrifice was humility, so they said in the Zohar (parashat Pinchas 240b), the beginning of a sacrifice is at the time a person confesses his sins upon it, and it is slaughtered and its blood is sprinkled on the altar. — end. Further, on p. 241a: Adam [man] is engraved on the Throne — Adam is the essence of everything — and there he offers his spirit and his soul. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:42: It says in the Yerushalmi, chapter "Keitzad" (Ta'anit, ch. 2, halachah 1), in these words: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda expounded, "let us lift our hearts with our hands" (Lamentations 3:41) — and is it possible for a person to take his heart and place it within his hand? Rather, what is "nisa" [lift]? Let us make ["neshavei"] our hearts like our palms, and then "to God in heaven" — so too, if there is an impure creeping thing in a person's hand, even if he immerses in the waters of Shiloach or the waters of creation, he has no purification ever — remove it from his hand, and immediately he is pure. — end of quotation. The intent is that just as the hands must have no impure creeping thing — namely, sin — so too the heart must be like the palms, clean of thinking to commit a transgression, as it is said (Isaiah 55:7), "let the wicked forsake his way and the man of iniquity his thoughts" — and "nisa" is a term for equalizing, as in "neshavei."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:43: Also, the essence of a fast, especially a communal fast, requires the examination of one's deeds, as it is said (Lamentations 3:40), "let us search and examine our ways and return to the Lord" — it appears that there is no way to repentance, of which it is said "return, O Israel, to the Lord," except through the investigation and examination of one's deeds. And this is the essence of the fast, as the prophet Isaiah, peace be upon him, said, in the passage where he says (Isaiah 58:3), "why have we fasted, and You do not see; we have afflicted our soul, and You do not know," and he says afterward, "is such the fast I choose, a day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow down his head like a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes beneath him? Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the Lord? Is not this the fast that I choose: to loosen the chains of wickedness, to undo the bonds of the yoke?" And the first verse, saying "is such the fast I choose," etc., "a day of affliction," etc., "to bow down like a bulrush," etc., is in the interrogative, in astonishment — meaning, none of this is acceptable before Him; but the chosen fast is "to loosen the chains of wickedness."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:44: So too it is explained in the Yerushalmi, chapter 2 of Ta'aniyot (halachah 1), in these words: Rabbi Elazar said, "is such the fast I choose" — rather, "a day for a man to afflict his soul" — this is not the fast that I desire; and what fast do I desire? "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loosen the chains of wickedness, to undo the bonds of the yoke; is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the poor who are cast out into your house?" What is written after it? "Then you shall call, and the Lord shall answer," etc. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:45: It follows that the totality of a fast requires the examination of deeds, the abandonment of sin, and the giving of charity for its own sake, as is explained in this verse, which contains several aspects requiring precision in the verse, all of which pertain to the matter of charity.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:46: So too it is explained in Tractate Ta'anit (12b) regarding what is written in Ezra, when he decreed a fast upon them (Nehemiah 9:3), "and they read from the book of the Torah of God for a quarter of the day," etc., in these words: Abaye said, on a fast day, from morning until midday they examine the matters of the city, and from midday, a quarter of the day they read [Scripture] and are dismissed, and a quarter of the day they seek mercy, as it is said, "and they read from the book of the Torah of God for a quarter of the day," and for the [next] quarter of the day they confess and prostrate themselves. But I shall reverse this — do not think so, for it is written, "and to me were gathered all who trembled." — end of quotation. Here, the first half of the day is devoted to the examination of deeds before Torah and prayer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:47: So too it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Vayechi 228b), on the verse (Isaiah 38:2), "and Hezekiah turned his face to the wall" — that one should not pray about his sin until he has set his whole attention to rectify his iniquity — in these words, briefly: from here we learn that whoever has a sin and wishes to seek mercy over it, should direct his face and his thoughts to rectify himself from that sin, and afterward seek his prayer, in the manner of (Lamentations 3:40), "let us search and examine our ways and return to the Lord" — "let us search our ways" first, and afterward "let us return." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:48: Regarding the matter of charity, they said in Sanhedrin (35a): Rabbi Elazar said, any fast in which charity is delayed overnight is as though [one who fasts] sheds blood, as it is said (Isaiah 1:21), "righteousness [charity] lodged in her, but now murderers." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:49: In Sefer Chasidim (siman 226) it is written: know and understand, although the sages said, fasting is good for a [bad] dream like fire for tow, they said this only for those who repent along with the fasting. Behold, a certain Jew saw a dream on the night of the ninth of Tishrei, and fasted on the ninth and on Yom Kippur — that is two days and a night — and it did not help him, because they show him a harsh dream so that he examine his deeds, for a fast is in place of a sin-offering. Just as a sacrifice does not avail without repentance, as it is said (Proverbs 21:27), "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination," so a fast for a dream does not avail without repentance. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:50: Rabbeinu Tam wrote in Sefer HaYashar that on the day of the fast one must be careful of anger, because bile grows dominant. And so it is also written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 617): when a person fasts, he should guard himself from being irritable that day, for when a person is hungry he is irritable, and if he becomes angry, it would be better for him not to fast, but rather to be satiated and good-hearted toward people, so that he not quarrel — and it is written (Isaiah 58:4), "behold, you fast for strife and contention, and to strike with a wicked fist; do not fast as you do today," etc. And the early ones, when they fasted, would eat only with salt and drink water, like Rabbi Yehoshua, who spoke against Beit Shammai (Chagigah 22b). — end of quotation.
